javascript-quill-reverse-tabnabbing.commentary: The version string matches the advisory and the code does not. Quill before 1.3.7 created editor links with target="_blank" and no rel attribute, so the page you opened could rewrite the address of the page you came from. The copy Vaadin ships is built from 1.3.6 and says so in its header, which is what your scanner read, but the link handler in it already sets rel="noopener noreferrer" before it sets the target. Nothing to upgrade.
javascript-quill-reverse-tabnabbing.impact: None. The attribute the advisory asks for is already on the links the editor creates.

maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-classic-rec.commentary: This needs a logback component nobody turns on. The receiver listens on a socket for log events sent by another process and deserialises them, and a crafted stream makes it allocate without bound. It exists only if your logback configuration declares a SocketReceiver or a ServerSocketReceiver, which a Vaadin application does not, and which the Spring Boot default configuration does not either. Look in your logback.xml: if there is no receiver element, nothing is listening.
maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-classic-rec.fix_expected: None from any Spring Boot you can download: Maven Central ends the 2.7 line at 2.7.18, which pins logback 1.2.12, and later 2.7 releases, 2.7.35 today, are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support.
maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-classic-rec.impact: None unless the logback configuration opens a receiver socket. There whoever can reach that port exhausts the heap.
maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-classic-rec.workaround: Nothing, unless your logback configuration declares a receiver. If it does, add <logback.version>1.2.13</logback.version> to the properties of your pom. Measured on 2026-10-24 on 14.14.8 and 23.6.17: logback-classic and logback-core move from 1.2.12 to 1.2.13 and slf4j-api stays at 1.7.36, which the 1.2 line needs. Only resolution was measured, not a running application.

maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-core-1-2-x.commentary: Real. Vaadin 14 and 23 run on Spring Boot 2.7.18, which pins logback 1.2.12, and all eight of these are in range for it according to the advisory database. Two are fixed inside the same 1.2 line and the other six are not: their fixes are in 1.3, 1.5 and later, and those lines need SLF4J 2, which Spring Boot 2.7 does not use. So the easy half of this is one property and the other half is a larger move, described below.
maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-core-1-2-x.fix_expected: The logback 1.2 line itself ends at 1.2.13. Spring Boot 2.7.18 is the last 2.7 release on Maven Central, later ones are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support, and no Vaadin 14 or 23 release moves the version either.
maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-core-1-2-x.impact: Every Vaadin 14 and 23 application, since logback is the logging backend Spring Boot configures by default. Two are high and both are fixed by the cheap step. What the six that remain cost depends on what you log and what reaches a configuration file: most of them are reached through logback's own configuration or its serialised event receivers, not through ordinary logging calls.
maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-core-1-2-x.workaround: Set the logback.version property in your own pom to 1.2.13. Measured on 2026-10-18 on 23.6.16: the override resolves, and by the advisory database it takes the eight down to six, clearing both high ones, CVE-2023-6378 and CVE-2023-6481. 1.2.13 is the end of that line, so the remaining six need logback 1.5.34, which clears all eight and which this measurement will not recommend on its own: logback 1.3 and later implement the SLF4J 2 provider interface, and the same resolution shows slf4j-api staying at 1.7.36 when only logback.version is raised, which is the combination that leaves an application with no logging backend at runtime. Moving slf4j too is a real option and it was not verified here, so verify it in your own application before shipping it.

maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-core-24-4.commentary: Real on 24.4, and one property clears all six. Vaadin 24.4.26 declares Spring Boot 3.2.12, which pins logback 1.4.14, and the advisory database lists all six against that version. Spring Boot 3.2.12 is the last release of the 3.2 line published to Maven Central, so no patch of it is coming to raise logback and no release of Vaadin 24.4 can move a version Spring Boot manages. Unlike on Vaadin 14 and 23, the move to logback 1.5 is free here: 24.4 already resolves SLF4J 2, which is what the 1.5 line needs.
maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-core-24-4.fix_expected: No further Spring Boot 3.2 release will carry it: Maven Central ends that line at 3.2.12, and Broadcom, which took it to 3.2.19 under commercial Spring support, has ended it too. The version only moves when you set it or when you move to a newer Spring Boot.
maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-core-24-4.impact: Every Vaadin 24.4 application, since logback is the logging backend Spring Boot configures by default. None of the six is high or critical, and what they cost depends on what reaches a logback configuration file or a serialised event receiver rather than on ordinary logging calls: four are deserialisation or class instantiation through logback own machinery, one is expression language injection in a configuration file and one is a server side request forgery when the configuration names a remote resource.
maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-core-24-4.workaround: Set the logback.version property in your own pom to 1.5.38, the newest of that line, which the advisory database reports clean, and take it out once you move to a Spring Boot that pins a fixed logback itself. Measured on 2026-10-24 on 24.4.26 against Spring Boot 3.2.12: it moves logback-core and logback-classic together from 1.4.14 to 1.5.38, and slf4j-api stays at 2.0.16, which is the version the 1.5 line needs. That is the trap the same verdict on Vaadin 14 and 23 warns about and it does not apply here.

maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-core-24-7.commentary: Real on 24.7, and one property clears all three. Vaadin 24.7.17 declares Spring Boot 3.4.13, which pins logback 1.5.22, and the advisory database lists these three against that version. Spring Boot 3.4.13 is the last release of the 3.4 line published to Maven Central, so no patch of it is coming to raise logback and no release of Vaadin 24.7 can move a version Spring Boot manages.
maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-core-24-7.fix_expected: No further Spring Boot 3.4 release will arrive on Maven Central: the line ends there at 3.4.13, and later releases, 3.4.18 today, are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support. The version only moves when you set it or when you move to a newer Spring Boot.
maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-core-24-7.impact: Every Vaadin 24.7 application, since logback is the logging backend Spring Boot configures by default. All three are low, and all three are reached through logback own deserialisation and class instantiation machinery rather than through ordinary logging calls: an application that does not enable a socket receiver and does not let untrusted input reach its logback configuration has no path to them.
maven-ch-qos-logback-logback-core-24-7.workaround: Set the logback.version property in your own pom to 1.5.38, the newest of that line, which the advisory database reports clean, and take it out once you move to a Spring Boot that pins a fixed logback itself. Measured on 2026-10-24 on 24.7.17 against Spring Boot 3.4.13: it moves logback-core and logback-classic together from 1.5.22 to 1.5.38, and slf4j-api stays at 2.0.17.

maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.commentary: Real on Vaadin 14 and 23. Both run on Spring Boot 2.7.18, which pins jackson-core at 2.13.5, and the advisory database answers these three for that version. No vaadin-bom of either line manages Jackson and Spring Boot 2.7 has no later free release, so the property below is the fix. Vaadin's own UI traffic on these lines is parsed with elemental.json, so these apply where Jackson reads JSON from outside: your REST controllers and anything else of yours that parses JSON. The 2.14.2 also reported on some 23.6 releases is the Vaadin Maven plugin's build classpath and is not deployed.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.fix_expected: None from any Spring Boot you can download: Maven Central ends the 2.7 line at 2.7.18, and later 2.7 releases are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support, so the property is the only route on Vaadin 14 and 23.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.impact: None where no endpoint of yours reads JSON with Jackson. Where one does, a crafted JSON document is a denial of service.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.workaround: Set <jackson-bom.version>2.18.12</jackson-bom.version> in the properties of your own pom, and take it out once your Spring Boot pins a fixed Jackson itself.

maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.commentary: Real on 24.4 and 24.7. Their Spring Boot pins jackson-core: 3.2.12 gives 2.15.4 on 24.4 and 3.4.13 gives 2.18.5 on 24.7. The advisory database answers CVE-2026-18401 and CVE-2026-68494 for both and CVE-2026-89407 for 2.18.5 only. Neither Spring Boot line has a later public release, so the property below is the fix. On these two series Vaadin's UI request handling does not use Jackson; Hilla endpoints and your own JSON endpoints do. The first two advisories concern only Jackson's non blocking parser, which Spring uses in its reactive JSON decoder.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.fix_expected: None from any Spring Boot you can download: Maven Central ends the 3.2 and 3.4 lines at 3.2.12 and 3.4.13, and later releases are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support. No Vaadin release moves this version.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.impact: None from CVE-2026-18401 and CVE-2026-68494 unless input is read through Spring's reactive decoder, as WebFlux and WebClient do. CVE-2026-89407 applies to any parsed number. In both cases a crafted JSON document is a denial of service.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.workaround: Set <jackson-bom.version>2.18.12</jackson-bom.version> in the properties of your own pom. It stays on Jackson 2.18, the line Spring Boot 3.4 uses, and clears every Jackson 2 advisory reported on these two series. Take it out once your Spring Boot pins a fixed version itself.

maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.commentary: The version is your Spring Boot's: 3.5.16, the newest 3.5 release, pins jackson-core 2.21.4, and no Vaadin release moves it. On this series Flow does call Jackson's parser on every UI request, including on event data your browser chooses, but the vulnerable regular expression is not on that path: it runs only when Jackson converts a JSON string into a float, double, BigDecimal or Number, and Flow never does that with what the browser sends. Hilla endpoints and signals, a ReactAdapterComponent of your own and your own JSON endpoints do, which is why this stays a risk until your Spring Boot pins a fixed Jackson.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.fix_expected: A Spring Boot 3.5 release that pins Jackson 2.21.7. Maven Central has none as of 2026-11-02, and no Vaadin release moves this version.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.impact: None unless your application binds JSON from the browser to a float, double, BigDecimal or Number through Jackson: a Hilla endpoint or signal, a ReactAdapterComponent of your own, or your own REST controller. There, a crafted number sent as a string makes the request spend excessive CPU.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.workaround: Set <jackson-bom.version>2.21.7</jackson-bom.version> in the properties of your own pom, and take it out once your Spring Boot pins a fixed Jackson itself.

maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.commentary: The jar is in your application and the flawed code in it is not reached. CVE-2026-89425 is in UTF8DataInputJsonParser, which Jackson builds only for a java.io.DataInput source, and only bites while reporting an invalid token. On 24.9 and 24.10 Vaadin does give browser data to Jackson, for example the history state of every navigation, but as a String that elemental.json has already parsed and written back, so it is valid JSON and goes to a different parser. Nothing on the 24 series classpaths outside Jackson hands it a DataInput. Code of your own that calls createParser(DataInput) is outside this answer.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.impact: None through Vaadin or Spring on the 24 series. Your own code that parses a DataInput with Jackson is a separate question.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.workaround: None needed, unless your own code parses a java.io.DataInput with Jackson.

maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.commentary: The version is your Spring Boot's: 3.5.16, the newest 3.5 release, pins jackson-core 2.21.4, and no Vaadin release moves it. On this series Flow does call Jackson's parser on every UI request, including on event data your browser chooses, but the vulnerable regular expression is not on that path: it runs only when Jackson converts a JSON string into a float, double, BigDecimal or Number, and Flow never does that with what the browser sends. Hilla endpoints and signals, a ReactAdapterComponent of your own and your own JSON endpoints do, which is why this stays a risk until your Spring Boot pins a fixed Jackson.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.fix_expected: A Spring Boot 3.5 release that pins Jackson 2.21.7. Maven Central has none as of 2026-11-02, and no Vaadin release moves this version.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.impact: None unless your application binds JSON from the browser to a float, double, BigDecimal or Number through Jackson: a Hilla endpoint or signal, a ReactAdapterComponent of your own, or your own REST controller. There, a crafted number sent as a string makes the request spend excessive CPU.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.workaround: Set <jackson-bom.version>2.21.7</jackson-bom.version> in the properties of your own pom, and take it out once your Spring Boot pins a fixed Jackson itself.

maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.commentary: The Jackson your scanner found is on the classpath of the widgetset plugin and the application you deploy carries none: Vaadin 7 and 8 are servlet applications with no JSON binding in them. vaadin-maven-plugin declares resteasy-client and resteasy-jackson2-provider 6.2.11.Final directly, which is what brings jackson-core 2.18.1. All four advisories are denials of service on a crafted document: a number token of unbounded length that the async parser fails to constrain, quadratic backtracking in the float pattern of looksLikeValidNumber, and two more of that family. Every one of them needs the build to parse JSON somebody hostile wrote. The only goal here that makes an HTTP request at all is the widgetset compilation when you ask it for the CDN mode, and the client it drives is compiled against javax.ws.rs while every Jackson provider on this classpath implements jakarta.ws.rs, so they cannot serve its response. Everything else the build reads is your own project. The war you deploy resolves no Jackson on any path.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no Jackson. On the build machine all four need a hostile JSON document to reach the parser, and a widgetset build parses JSON from nowhere.

maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.commentary: The report says Jackson overflows the stack when asked to serialise an object that contains itself, such as a Map that holds a reference to itself. Jackson's maintainers rejected it as a vulnerability and the CVE record carries the disputed tag: an attacker cannot build a cyclic Java object through a request, only your own code can. Scanners flag every jackson-databind before 2.16.0 because that release added a limit on write nesting. Nothing has to be upgraded for it.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.impact: None from outside. It needs code of yours to hand Jackson an object graph that refers to itself, which fails whatever the version.

maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.commentary: Real on Vaadin 14 and 23. Both run on Spring Boot 2.7.18, which pins jackson-databind at 2.13.5, and the advisory database answers these for that version; CVE-2026-68497 only for the 2.14.2 the Vaadin Maven plugin uses at build time. No vaadin-bom of either line manages Jackson and Spring Boot 2.7 has no later free release, so the property below is the fix. Vaadin's own UI traffic on these lines is parsed with elemental.json, so these apply where Jackson binds JSON from outside into your types: REST controllers and anything else of yours that deserialises JSON.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.fix_expected: None from any Spring Boot you can download: Maven Central ends the 2.7 line at 2.7.18, and later 2.7 releases are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support, so the property is the only route on Vaadin 14 and 23.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.impact: None of the class instantiation unless you enable polymorphic typing, and none of the DNS lookups to attacker chosen hosts unless you bind InetAddress or InetSocketAddress. What remains depends on what you deserialise and is a denial of service.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.workaround: Set <jackson-bom.version>2.18.12</jackson-bom.version> in the properties of your own pom, and take it out once your Spring Boot pins a fixed Jackson itself.

maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.commentary: This one needs two annotations on the same property and a Vaadin application has neither together. When a property carries both @JsonView and @JsonUnwrapped, Jackson replays the buffered JSON for the unwrapped part without checking the active view, so a field meant to be invisible under that view can be written from the incoming document. It needs your own code to deserialise such a type from input somebody else controls. Vaadin does not: it parses requests with elemental.json, its own library, and the only Vaadin classes that use @JsonUnwrapped at all are two in Charts, which are written out to the browser rather than read from it, and no Vaadin class uses @JsonView.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.impact: None through Vaadin. An application whose own REST controllers deserialise a type carrying both annotations under an active view is affected, and that is the reader's own code rather than anything the framework registers.

maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.commentary: Real on 24.4 and 24.7. Their Spring Boot pins jackson-databind: 3.2.12 gives 2.15.4 on 24.4 and 3.4.13 gives 2.18.5 on 24.7, and the advisory database answers all four for both. Neither Spring Boot line has a later public release, so the property below is the fix. On these two series Vaadin's UI request handling does not use Jackson; Hilla endpoints and your own JSON endpoints bind request bodies with it, and that is where these apply.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.fix_expected: None from any Spring Boot you can download: Maven Central ends the 3.2 and 3.4 lines at 3.2.12 and 3.4.13, and later releases are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support. No Vaadin release moves this version.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.impact: None from three of them unless polymorphic typing is enabled on your ObjectMapper, where they instantiate unexpected classes, CVE-2026-110879 being the incomplete fix follow-up of CVE-2026-54512 with the same condition. Of the other two, one makes the server resolve an attacker chosen host when binding InetSocketAddress, and one lets a record property marked @JsonIgnore be set.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.workaround: Set <jackson-bom.version>2.18.12</jackson-bom.version> in the properties of your own pom. It stays on Jackson 2.18, the line Spring Boot 3.4 uses, and clears every Jackson 2 advisory reported on these two series. Take it out once your Spring Boot pins a fixed version itself.

maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.commentary: These need JSON from the browser bound to a Java type that uses a particular Jackson feature. Flow itself only builds trees from browser data: on 24.9 and 24.10, event data, history state and @ClientCallable arguments go through readTree into a JsonNode, which binds nothing. Binding happens into types you write: Hilla endpoint parameters, ReactAdapterComponent state, signal values, Spring controllers. Check those types for a Path, InetAddress, Duration or XMLGregorianCalendar property, @JsonView, @JsonUnwrapped, @JsonIdentityInfo, @JsonTypeInfo or default typing, or ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES. Copilot also binds messages from its browser panel into its own types, some with a Path property: if copilot is on your production classpath, treat this as a risk.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.impact: None unless one of your own types bound from browser JSON uses one of those features, or copilot runs in production. Where it does, the advisory is a denial of service, a property set that should have been ignored, or a lookup the server should not make.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.workaround: If one of your types meets a condition above, set <jackson-bom.version>2.18.12</jackson-bom.version> on 24.4 and 24.7, or <jackson-bom.version>2.21.7</jackson-bom.version> on 24.9 and 24.10, in the properties of your own pom. These are the properties the jackson-databind risk verdicts for those series carry, measured on 2026-10-24.

maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.commentary: The Jackson data binding your scanner found is on the classpath of the widgetset plugin and the application you deploy carries none: Vaadin 7 and 8 are servlet applications with no JSON binding in them. vaadin-maven-plugin declares resteasy-jackson2-provider 6.2.11.Final directly, which is what brings jackson-databind 2.18.1. The thirteen are of two kinds and neither one happens here. Most are bypasses of an annotation that was supposed to keep a field out, @JsonView, @JsonIgnore or a type id on a creator property, which need an application that binds JSON from an outside party onto its own annotated classes. The rest are denials of service on a crafted document. The build binds no JSON to anything: the only goal that speaks to a server is the widgetset compilation in CDN mode, whose client is compiled against javax.ws.rs while every Jackson provider here implements jakarta.ws.rs. The war you deploy resolves no Jackson on any path.
maven-com-fasterxml-jackson-core-jackson.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no Jackson. On the build machine every one of the thirteen needs JSON from somebody hostile to be bound onto a class, and the widgetset build binds none.

maven-com-google-guava-guava-14-build.commentary: The old Guava is on your build machine and the application does not deploy any Guava at all. The four advisories are reported against 20.0, which the Maven plugin that builds the frontend resolves through a reflection library it uses to scan classes. What your application resolves is 31.1-jre, and at test scope, so it is not in the archive you deploy. Two of the four are about a temporary directory created with permissions that let other local users read it, and the other two are memory exhaustion when reading an untrusted serialised object. Nothing to do.
maven-com-google-guava-guava-14-build.impact: None in a deployed application. On a build machine, the temporary directory ones need another local user on the same host.

maven-com-jcraft-jsch-8-build.commentary: The JSch your scanner found is dragged onto the build classpath of Vaadin 8 by a Maven 2 era deploy transport, and the application you deploy carries none. The advisory is a path traversal in JSch's sftp client: a recursive download from a malicious ssh server can write files outside the target directory. On Vaadin 8 the widgetset plugin carries maven-core 2.0.6 as the API maven-archiver links against, and that old maven-core declares wagon-ssh, the transport Maven 2 used to deploy artifacts over scp, which is what brings jsch 0.1.27 at runtime scope. A widgetset compilation opens no ssh connection and downloads nothing over sftp; the transports your own build deploys with come from the Maven installation you run. The war you deploy resolves no JSch on any path.
maven-com-jcraft-jsch-8-build.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no JSch. On the build machine the traversal needs the build to perform a recursive sftp download from an ssh server somebody hostile controls, which the widgetset compilation never does.

maven-com-vaadin-flow-maven-plugin-2026-.commentary: Real on 24.4 and 24.7, and not fixed in any release of either line. When the frontend build fails, the library the build plugin used to run it put the whole process environment into the error it raised, so the environment ends up in the build log. The fix removes that library, and it is in flow-maven-plugin 24.9.18 and later. Vaadin 24.4.26 and 24.7.17, the newest releases of these lines, resolve flow-maven-plugin 24.4.20 and 24.7.17, and both still carry it. This is your build log, not your application.
maven-com-vaadin-flow-maven-plugin-2026-.fix_expected: No release of 24.4 or 24.7 is announced with the fix. Flow 24.4.21 and 24.7.18, published to Maven Central on 2026-10-21 and not yet in a Vaadin release, still declare the library.
maven-com-vaadin-flow-maven-plugin-2026-.impact: None in the deployed application. On 24.4 and 24.7 a build whose frontend step fails prints every environment variable of that build, which on a continuous integration service is often readable by more people than the secrets were meant for.
maven-com-vaadin-flow-maven-plugin-2026-.workaround: Keep secrets out of the environment the Maven build runs in, passing them another way, and restrict who can read build logs. No property turns the logging off.

maven-com-vaadin-flow-server-2026-2742-1.commentary: The published advisory says this artifact is fixed in a version it has never had. CVE-2026-2742 lets a request to a reserved framework path create a session without authenticating, and on the Vaadin 14 line the fix is flow-server 2.13.1, which Vaadin 14.14.1 and later resolve. The record scanners read says com.vaadin:flow-server is fixed in 14.14.1, a Vaadin platform number rather than a flow-server one, so a scanner comparing 2.13.8 against it concludes you are behind. You are not. Nothing to upgrade on this count.
maven-com-vaadin-flow-server-2026-2742-1.impact: None on Vaadin 14.14.1 and later, which resolve flow-server 2.13.1 or newer.

maven-com-vaadin-flow-server-2026-2742-s.commentary: Your scanner is right that the advisory names your version and wrong that your version is affected, from 24.7.16 on. CVE-2026-2742 lets a request to a reserved framework path create a session without authenticating. The fix was backported to the 24.7 line as flow-server 24.7.15, which Vaadin 24.7.16 and later resolve, but the advisory still gives all of 24 below 24.9.8 one range, so every 24.7 release stays flagged. On 24.7.16 or later there is nothing to do. Below 24.7.16 the finding is real and you upgrade within 24.7, to 24.7.16 or later.
maven-com-vaadin-flow-server-2026-2742-s.impact: None on 24.7.16 and later. Below it, a request to a reserved path creates a session without authentication.
maven-com-vaadin-flow-server-2026-2742-s.workaround: On a release below 24.7.16, upgrade to Vaadin 24.7.16 or later; 24.7.17 is the newest.

maven-com-vaadin-vaadin-2025-15022-stale.commentary: Your scanner is right that the advisory names your version and wrong that your version is affected, from 24.7.15 on. Below it the finding is real and you upgrade within 24.7.

maven-io-opentelemetry-opentelemetry-api.commentary: OpenTelemetry reaches a deployed Vaadin 24 application only through Observability Kit; TestBench brings the same jar at test scope. An oversized W3C baggage header makes the parser allocate without a bound, and baggage propagation is on by default. Which release decides the version depends on the shape of the application. With Spring Boot its dependency management pins 1.31.0 on 24.4, 1.43.0 on 24.7 and 1.49.0 on 24.9 and 24.10, all affected. Without Spring Boot the version is the one the Observability Kit the platform pins carries: 1.23.0 on 24.4 through kit 3.0.0 and 1.44.1 on 24.7 through kit 3.1.0, both affected, while 24.9 and 24.10 pin kit 3.2.1, which carries 1.62.0, so that shape is already past it. The 25 series resolve 1.62.0, which is fixed.
maven-io-opentelemetry-opentelemetry-api.fix_expected: With Spring Boot, on 24.4 and 24.7 none from any Spring Boot you can download: Maven Central ends those lines at 3.2.12 and 3.4.13, which pin 1.31.0 and 1.43.0, and later releases are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support. On 24.9 and 24.10 a Spring Boot 3.5 patch pinning 1.62.0, which does not exist yet: 3.5.16, the newest open one, pins 1.49.0. Without Spring Boot, 24.9 and 24.10 already resolve 1.62.0 through Observability Kit 3.2.1 and need nothing, and on 24.4 and 24.7 the exit is an Observability Kit release built for those lines, a 3.1.1 from the 3.1.0 tag carrying a fixed OpenTelemetry, and a platform release pinning it on both branches. Kit 3.2.1 and later cannot be that release: they fail at startup on any Flow before 24.9.
maven-io-opentelemetry-opentelemetry-api.impact: None unless a Vaadin 24 application declares observability-kit-starter and whoever can send a baggage header can reach it. There it is a denial of service through memory and CPU, not a way in.
maven-io-opentelemetry-opentelemetry-api.workaround: With Spring Boot, set <opentelemetry.version>1.62.0</opentelemetry.version> in your pom; take it out once your Spring Boot pins 1.62.0 or later. Without Spring Boot that property moves nothing, because only Spring Boot's dependency management reads it: import io.opentelemetry:opentelemetry-bom 1.62.0 in dependencyManagement. Do not declare observability-kit-starter 3.2.1 yourself on 24.4 or 24.7: since 3.2.0 its license listener extends a Flow class that first ships in flow-server 24.9, the listener is a registered service init listener, and the application fails at startup with NoClassDefFoundError. In every case resolution was measured, not compatibility with Observability Kit. If you do not use baggage, otel.propagators=tracecontext drops the baggage propagator instead. These moves change the jar your application resolves and not the copy inside the Observability Kit agent, which carries its own: the 3.2.1 and 4.1.2 agents carry OpenTelemetry 1.62.0 and 1.65.0, both past this one, and the 3.0.0 and 3.1.0 agents carry 1.23.0 and 1.44.1, which are not.

maven-io-opentelemetry-opentelemetry-api.commentary: The copy that matters is not the one your scanner found. OpenTelemetry reaches a deployed Vaadin 24 application through Observability Kit, and Observability Kit 3 works through a Java agent that carries its own OpenTelemetry inside it. That agent extracts the W3C trace context of every incoming request with the tracestate parser this advisory describes: a long run of spaces or tabs costs CPU that grows with the square of its length. Agents up to 3.2.1 carry it, because the parser comes from the upstream Java agent the kit is built on rather than from the OpenTelemetry version it declares; the 3.2.2 agent, published on 2026-11-11, carries the rewritten parser, so what remains exposed is an agent older than that. The opentelemetry-api jar your scanner reports is a different copy, and nothing in a Vaadin application passes it an incoming header unless your own code does. Without Observability Kit that jar arrives only through TestBench, which parses no incoming header.
maven-io-opentelemetry-opentelemetry-api.fix_expected: The observability-kit-agent 3.2.2 on Maven Central, published on 2026-11-11, built on the upstream Java agent 2.33.1, whose shaded parser scans the header instead of compiling a pattern for it.
maven-io-opentelemetry-opentelemetry-api.impact: None unless the application runs an Observability Kit agent older than 3.2.2, or code of its own extracts trace context from incoming requests. There anybody who can send a request can make each one cost CPU through a crafted tracestate header, a denial of service and not a way in.
maven-io-opentelemetry-opentelemetry-api.workaround: Update the agent to observability-kit-agent 3.2.2 from Maven Central; it is the jar the JVM is started with, so no application rebuild is involved. Until then, cap or remove the tracestate header at your proxy or load balancer before requests reach the application, or start the agent with -Dotel.propagators=none if you do not need trace context from upstream callers. Raising opentelemetry.version in your pom moves the jar your scanner reports and does not change the agent.

maven-io-opentelemetry-opentelemetry-api.commentary: The parser is in the jar and nothing in a Vaadin application hands it an incoming header. From 25.3, opentelemetry-api 1.62.0 arrives through TestBench, whose Selenium client only adds trace context to the requests it sends, and Observability Kit no longer uses OpenTelemetry or an agent. The advisory needs incoming tracestate headers to reach W3CTraceContextPropagator.extract, which happens only if you add tracing of your own: Spring Boot OpenTelemetry tracing, the OpenTelemetry Java agent, or code that extracts trace context from requests.
maven-io-opentelemetry-opentelemetry-api.impact: None unless your application adds tracing that extracts W3C trace context from incoming requests. There anybody who can send a request can make each one cost CPU through a crafted tracestate header.
maven-io-opentelemetry-opentelemetry-api.workaround: If you add such tracing, set <opentelemetry.version>1.67.0</opentelemetry.version> in your pom, which resolves the api and the SDK at 1.67.0 under the Spring Boot parent, or cap or remove the tracestate header at your proxy before requests reach the application.

This advisory is narrower than the other four on the same jar: it is a timing channel in FrodoEngine and only affects the decapsulation step of the FrodoKEM algorithm. Of the 424 jars on that classpath, only bcprov itself names FrodoKEM, and only from its own key factories and its post quantum provider registration. The JCA route needs BouncyCastlePQCProvider installed, which nothing on the classpath does, and the plain BouncyCastleProvider that nimbus-jose-jwt and the fabric8 Kubernetes client do install does not register Frodo at all. Reaching this code means writing it in your own application.
maven-org-bouncycastle-bcprov-jdk18on-24.fix_expected: No Vaadin 24.7 release will move the version, because Control Center is no longer developed. The 24.9 and 24.10 lines pin a Control Center that resolves bcprov-jdk18on 1.85, and an application that does not declare control-center-starter resolves no Bouncy Castle on 24.7 at all.
maven-org-bouncycastle-bcprov-jdk18on-24.impact: None unless your own code performs FrodoKEM decapsulation, either through BouncyCastlePQCProvider or by calling FrodoKEMExtractor directly. Nothing Vaadin, Control Center or Spring puts on a 24.7 classpath does either. Where it is reached, the time the decapsulation takes leaks what the algorithm is meant to keep secret, which is why the advisory scores confidentiality high; its own CVSS v4 vector records the exploit maturity as unproven.
maven-org-bouncycastle-bcprov-jdk18on-24.workaround: None needed for this advisory. If you already applied the bcprov-jdk18on 1.85 override that answers the other four advisories on this jar, it clears this one too: osv.dev reports nothing at all against 1.85, asked on 2026-11-06.

maven-org-codehaus-jackson-jackson-mappe.commentary: Not in what you deploy. jackson-mapper-asl is Jackson 1, out of maintenance since 2013, and on Vaadin 14 it arrives only on the classpath of the Vaadin Maven plugin, through the frontend-plugin-core library that installs Node.js during the build. Your application does not resolve it, so nothing you ship contains it.
maven-org-codehaus-jackson-jackson-mappe.impact: None in a deployed application. It runs on your build machine, inside the Maven plugin.

maven-org-codehaus-plexus-plexus-utils-2.commentary: These reach the machine that builds a 23.6 application, not the application. plexus-utils 3.0.22 is on the classpath of the Vaadin Maven plugin, and it is inside the affected range, below 3.0.24. One advisory is a directory traversal when an archive is unpacked and the other is XML injection through a comment written unescaped, and nothing on that classpath calls either the unpacking class or the XML comment writer. Your deployed application does not contain plexus-utils at all.
maven-org-codehaus-plexus-plexus-utils-2.impact: None in a deployed application, and nothing in the build calls the affected code.

maven-org-codehaus-plexus-plexus-utils-2.commentary: This reaches the machine that builds a 23.6 application, not the application, and nothing there calls the affected code. The Vaadin Maven plugin brings plexus-utils 3.0.22, which is in the affected range, and no 23.6 release has moved it. The advisory is about Expand.extractFile unpacking an archive, and nothing on the plugin classpath calls Expand.

On the 24 series this reaches the application as well as the build, and nothing calls the affected code in either. App Sec Kit brings plexus-utils 3.4.2 into the application through maven-artifact on 24.4, 24.7, 24.9 up to 24.9.14 and 24.10.0 and 24.10.1, and the Vaadin Maven plugin brings 4.0.0 on 24.4, 24.7, 24.9 and 24.10 up to 24.10.11. Both are in the affected range. The advisory is about Expand.extractFile unpacking an archive, and nothing on either classpath calls Expand.
maven-org-codehaus-plexus-plexus-utils-2.fix_expected: Merged into flow main on 2026-10-07. It is not in a Vaadin release yet.
maven-org-codehaus-plexus-plexus-utils-2.impact: None. The vulnerable method is present and nothing in the application or the build calls it.

maven-org-codehaus-plexus-plexus-utils-7.commentary: The plexus-utils your scanner found is on your build machine and the application you deploy carries none. vaadin-maven-plugin, the plugin that compiles the widgetset on Vaadin 7 and 8, declares plexus-utils 4.0.2 directly and excludes the one maven-archiver would have brought. The advisory is a directory traversal in Expand.extractFile, which unpacks an archive and can write outside the target directory, and nothing on this classpath calls Expand: the only other holders of the name are the copies surefire shades under its own package, which are a different coordinate and not what the scanner reports. The war you deploy resolves no plexus-utils on any path. This is the same answer the 14, 23, 24 and 25 lines already carry for this advisory, measured again on this classpath.
maven-org-codehaus-plexus-plexus-utils-7.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries none. On the build machine the traversal needs something to call Expand.extractFile on an archive somebody hostile wrote, and no class of the widgetset build calls it at all.

maven-org-cyclonedx-cyclonedx-core-java-.commentary: This is about the XML half of a library that App Sec Kit uses for its JSON half. The advisory is an XML external entity hole in the validator that checks an XML bill of materials. App Sec Kit reads the bill of materials your build produced as JSON: the only classes of this library it refers to are the JSON parser, the model and the parse exception, and nothing else on the classpath touches the XML side. 24.9 and later resolve 11.0.1, which is fixed.
maven-org-cyclonedx-cyclonedx-core-java-.impact: None. The XML validator is never called, and the document App Sec Kit does read is the one your own build wrote.

maven-org-freemarker-freemarker-7-8-buil.commentary: The FreeMarker your scanner found belongs to a goal you run by hand in your IDE setup, and the application you deploy carries none. vaadin-maven-plugin declares freemarker 2.3.20 directly, and the only classes that touch it are EclipseMojo and EclipseTestMojo, the gwt:eclipse goals that write Eclipse launch configurations from templates shipped inside the plugin jar. A widgetset compilation never runs them. The advisory is a path traversal through the localized template lookup, which needs an attacker to name an arbitrary malformed locale identifier, and the lookup here is bounded twice over: the configuration loads templates with setClassForTemplateLoading, so the loader can only reach resources of the plugin jar itself, and the locale is the one the JVM is running under rather than anything an outside party chooses. The war you deploy resolves no FreeMarker on any path.
maven-org-freemarker-freemarker-7-8-buil.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no FreeMarker. On the build machine the traversal needs a malformed locale identifier from somebody hostile and a template loader that can reach the file they are after, and the only goal that loads a template reads templates out of the plugin jar under the JVM locale.

maven-org-iq80-snappy-snappy-7-8-build.commentary: The Snappy your scanner found is on your build machine and the application you deploy carries none. On Vaadin 7 and 8 the plugin that builds the widgetset resolves org.iq80.snappy 0.4 through plexus-archiver, the library Maven plugins use to pack and unpack archives, where it decompresses Snappy streams. The advisory is an out of bounds read while uncompressing crafted data, which crashes the JVM doing the uncompressing. The data the build decompresses comes from the archives of your own project and the artifacts your configured repositories serve, not from anything a user of the application sends. The war you deploy resolves no Snappy on any path.
maven-org-iq80-snappy-snappy-7-8-build.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no Snappy. On the build machine the crash needs the build to decompress data somebody hostile produced, and what it would crash is the build, not the application.

maven-org-jetbrains-kotlin-kotlin-stdlib.commentary: Your scanner has matched the wrong artifact. The advisory is unsafe deserialization of the incremental cache of KAPT, the annotation processing plugin of the Kotlin build tooling, and the advisory database names only org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-gradle-plugin. The CPE jetbrains:kotlin covers every artifact JetBrains publishes under that name, so the scanner reported it on kotlin-stdlib, which does not contain that code. The range is open because no version of kotlin-stdlib carries it. Nothing to upgrade for it.
maven-org-jetbrains-kotlin-kotlin-stdlib.impact: None. The affected code is build tooling and is not in this library.

maven-org-jetbrains-kotlin-kotlin-stdlib.commentary: The functions this advisory is about are still in the kotlin-stdlib the 24 series resolve, and nothing calls them. The advisory is createTempDir and createTempFile in kotlin.io creating files a local user can read. Kotlin 1.4.21 deprecated them and Kotlin 2.1.0 made them an error, which is why the advisory database says before 1.4.21 and NVD says before 2.1.0. The 24 series resolve 1.9.25, where they still exist, and no library on the classpath calls them. The 25 series resolve 2.3.21, outside both ranges.
maven-org-jetbrains-kotlin-kotlin-stdlib.impact: None. Nothing in the application calls the two deprecated functions.

maven-org-jsoup-jsoup-cleaner-and-xml.commentary: Vaadin does use jsoup, and each of these two needs something Vaadin does not do. CVE-2026-71497 is the Cleaner mis-parsing a malformed tag name that ends in a control character, and it bites only when the safelist you clean with permits a raw text element, which jsoup counts as iframe, noembed, noframes, script, style, textarea, title and xmp. Vaadin cleans with Safelist.none() in the action shortcut and the route not found page, with Safelist.relaxed() in the spreadsheet, the classic Panel and the appsec kit, and in the rich text editor with Safelist.basic() plus img, h1, h2, h3 and s. None of those permits any of the eight, and on these versions no Vaadin API accepts a safelist of yours, so the configuration the advisory describes cannot be reached through Vaadin at all. CVE-2026-75140 is the XML tree builder copying the inherited namespace map on every start element, so it needs you to be parsing XML with jsoup, and Vaadin parses HTML.
maven-org-jsoup-jsoup-cleaner-and-xml.impact: None through Vaadin. Two things are affected and both are your own code rather than ours, cleaning untrusted HTML with a safelist you built that permits a raw text element, and parsing untrusted XML with jsoup.

maven-org-springframework-boot-actuator-.commentary: Both need Actuator and one of your own endpoints that requires authentication placed under a path Actuator has taken: a health group additional path for CVE-2026-22731, or /cloudfoundryapplication for CVE-2026-22733. A plain Vaadin 24.7 starter does not bring Actuator; Control Center does. Even then the bypass needs that path collision, which you can check in your own configuration. Spring fixed both in Spring Boot 3.5.12. The 3.4 fix, 3.4.15, is sold under commercial support only, so 3.4.13, which 24.7.17 declares, is the last free release of that line.
maven-org-springframework-boot-actuator-.fix_expected: Vaadin 24.9 and later declare Spring Boot 3.5.16, which carries both fixes. No 3.4 release you can download will: Maven Central ends that line at 3.4.13, and the later 3.4 releases are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support.
maven-org-springframework-boot-actuator-.impact: None unless the application runs Actuator and declares an endpoint requiring authentication under a health group additional path or under /cloudfoundryapplication. There a request to that endpoint is served without authentication.
maven-org-springframework-boot-actuator-.workaround: Move any authenticated endpoint of your own out from under the paths set in management.endpoint.health.group.<name>.additional-path and out from under /cloudfoundryapplication.

maven-org-springframework-boot-devtools-.commentary: This one is about the DevTools remote debugging channel, which is off unless you set its secret. DevTools only runs in development, it is stripped from a repackaged application, and its remote support does nothing at all until spring.devtools.remote.secret is set. When it is set, the server compares the secret in a way that leaks its length through timing, and an attacker on the same network can eventually recover it and upload classes. If you have ever enabled remote DevTools against a deployed application, that is the configuration the advisory describes and it should not be deployed at all.
maven-org-springframework-boot-devtools-.fix_expected: None from the 3.4 line on Maven Central, which ends at 3.4.13: the later 3.4 releases are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support, and the advisory database marks the line affected up to 3.4.15 or 3.4.16 with no fixed release. The fixes are on 3.5.14 and 3.5.15, which are published, so the way out is a newer Spring Boot. Vaadin 24.9 and later declare 3.5.16.
maven-org-springframework-boot-devtools-.impact: None for an application built for production, which does not ship DevTools at all. It needs spring.devtools.remote.secret set and the DevTools endpoint exposed on a network an attacker can reach.
maven-org-springframework-boot-devtools-.workaround: Do not set spring.devtools.remote.secret on anything deployed. The Spring Boot repackage goal already excludes DevTools from the executable archive, so a production build has nothing to reach.

maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.commentary: The class this advisory is about is not in the jar it was reported on, and a Vaadin 24.4 application does not resolve the jar that holds it. EndpointRequest lives in spring-boot-actuator-autoconfigure, and 24.4.26 resolves no Actuator artifact. If you added Actuator yourself, the advisory applies only when all four of its conditions hold: you use Spring Security, a security rule uses EndpointRequest.to(), the endpoint it names is disabled or not exposed, and your application serves /null and needs it protected.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.fix_expected: Spring fixed it in Spring Boot 3.3.11 and 3.4.5; the 3.2 fix is commercial only and Maven Central ends 3.2 at 3.2.12. Vaadin 24.7 declares Spring Boot 3.4.13, which carries it.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.impact: None through spring-boot. With Actuator added and all four conditions met, the rule meant for that endpoint matches /null/** instead.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.workaround: Only if you added Actuator: keep the endpoints your EndpointRequest.to() rules name enabled and exposed, or write those rules against the literal path.

maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.commentary: This needs two things you would have to arrange: an attacker with a local account on the machine your application runs on, and server.servlet.session.persistent set to true. Spring Boot's ApplicationTemp picks a predictable directory under the system temporary directory without checking who owns it, and on the classpath of a Vaadin 14 or 23 application the only class that uses it is SessionStoreDirectory, which stores persisted HTTP sessions. Persistence is off by default. If you have turned it on, read the workaround.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.fix_expected: Nothing on a line these series can take. Spring fixed it in 2.7.33, which is behind commercial support; Maven Central's last free 2.7 release is 2.7.18.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.impact: None unless the application sets server.servlet.session.persistent to true and runs on a host shared with untrusted local users. There a local user who owns the directory first can read persisted session data to hijack logged in users, or plant a serialized object the application loads.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.workaround: Leave server.servlet.session.persistent at its default of false. If you need it, start the application with -Djava.io.tmpdir pointing at a directory only the application's user can write, created before the application starts.

maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.commentary: This is about an embedded message broker your application does not run. Spring Boot's ArtemisEmbeddedConfigurationFactory gives the embedded Artemis broker a fixed path for its data directory when none is configured, so on a shared host another local user can get there first. The autoconfiguration that uses it only runs when Artemis itself is on the classpath, and a Vaadin application does not bring it: you would have to add spring-boot-starter-artemis and run the broker embedded. If you do, configure the data directory explicitly.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.impact: None from anything a Vaadin application does on its own. It needs an embedded Artemis broker on a host shared with untrusted local users.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.workaround: Set the Artemis data directory explicitly if you embed the broker, rather than letting it default.

maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.commentary: Your scanner has matched the wrong product. This advisory is about Spring Tools 4 for Eclipse and the Spring Boot Tools extension for VSCode, which are editor tooling, and the dependency it was matched against is spring-boot-devtools, a different artifact that no editor ships. Nothing in a Vaadin application is affected, and nothing has to be upgraded for it.

This is the one advisory on this jar that is really about this jar, and it is about a feature nobody has switched on. Remote DevTools lets a developer push changes to an application running somewhere else, and the secret it compares is where the timing attack is. The whole server, the filter and the comparison exist only when the property spring.devtools.remote.secret is set, so an application that has never set it has no remote endpoint to attack. Check your own configuration for that property and for the SPRING_DEVTOOLS_REMOTE_SECRET environment variable. If you do use remote DevTools, it belongs on a development machine and never on anything reachable from outside.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.fix_expected: None from the 2.7 line on Maven Central, which ends at 2.7.18; later 2.7 releases are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support, and the advisory gives the line as last_affected at 2.7.32. Spring Boot fixed it in 3.5.14 and 4.0.6.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.impact: None for a deployed application, and none for a developer who has not set the property. Where remote DevTools is turned on, an attacker who can reach the application can learn the secret one character at a time from how long the answer takes, and the secret is what authorises pushing code into the running process.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.workaround: Do not set spring.devtools.remote.secret, which is the default. Nothing has to be removed or overridden to be in that state.

maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.commentary: Six Spring Boot advisories landed on this jar because the scanner matched the product name vmware:spring_boot, which every Spring Boot artifact carries. None of the six is about code in spring-boot-devtools. CVE-2026-22733 is about the Actuator CloudFoundry path, CVE-2026-40974 and CVE-2026-41001 about the Cassandra and Artemis auto-configuration in spring-boot-autoconfigure, and CVE-2026-40973, CVE-2026-40975 and CVE-2026-40977 about classes of the spring-boot jar. The ones about code your application carries are answered on those coordinates.

The class this advisory is about is not on your classpath. EndpointRequest is an Actuator API and lives in spring-boot-actuator, which a Vaadin application does not pull in, and the advisory's own conditions ask you to have called EndpointRequest.to() in a Spring Security chain. Vaadin never calls it. If you have added Actuator yourself and your security configuration uses EndpointRequest.to() against an endpoint that is disabled or not exposed, and your application serves a path /null that needs protecting, then read the advisory on spring-boot-actuator, because those four conditions are the whole of it.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.impact: None. The API cannot be called from an application that does not have it.

maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.commentary: These three are about auto-configurations that switch on only when their library is on your classpath, and a Vaadin 24.7 application resolves none of the three libraries. CVE-2026-40974 is the Cassandra SSL auto-configuration skipping hostname verification, CVE-2026-40992 is the mail auto-configuration skipping it, and CVE-2026-41001 is the embedded Artemis broker using a fixed, predictable data directory that another local user can create first. If you have added the Cassandra driver, a mail starter or embedded Artemis yourself, the workaround says what to set.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.fix_expected: Vaadin 24.9 and later declare Spring Boot 3.5.16, which carries all three: 3.5.14 fixed Cassandra, 3.5.15 mail and Artemis. Maven Central ends the 3.4 line at 3.4.13 with all three unfixed.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.impact: None through Vaadin. Applications that add one of those libraries: an attacker in the network path of the Cassandra or mail connection, or a local user taking over the Artemis data directory.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.workaround: Mail: set spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.ssl.checkserveridentity=true. Embedded Artemis: set spring.artemis.embedded.data-directory to a directory only the application's user can write. Cassandra: Spring names no property, so the way out is a Spring Boot that carries the fix.

maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.commentary: These three need something you have to turn on, and all three also need a local attacker on the same host. CVE-2026-40973 needs server.servlet.session.persistent set to true, which defaults to false, before a local attacker who controls the ApplicationTemp directory can read persisted sessions. CVE-2026-40977 needs ApplicationPidFileWriter registered, which Spring Boot does not register for you. CVE-2026-40975 is not a flaw in code that runs by itself at all: it says that the value of the ${random.value} property placeholder is not strong enough to be used as a secret, so it reaches you only if your own configuration uses it that way. Check your properties for ${random.value} behind anything that acts as a key or a password.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.fix_expected: None from the 3.4 line on Maven Central, which ends at 3.4.13: the later 3.4 releases are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support, and the advisory database marks the line affected up to 3.4.15 or 3.4.16 with no fixed release. The fixes are on 3.5.14 and 3.5.15, which are published, so the way out is a newer Spring Boot. Vaadin 24.9 and later declare 3.5.16.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.impact: None unless the application persists sessions to disk, registers the PID file writer, or uses ${random.value} where a secret is needed, and in the first two cases only against an attacker who already has a local account on the host.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.workaround: Leave server.servlet.session.persistent at its default of false, do not register ApplicationPidFileWriter, and replace any ${random.value} used as a secret with a value you generate and store yourself. Moving to Spring Boot 3.5.14 or newer fixes the first two in the framework.

maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.commentary: These two are about classes of the spring-boot jar your application carries, and both need something you would have to do. CVE-2026-40975 says values of ${random.value} are not strong enough to be secrets, so it reaches you only if your own properties put ${random.value} where a key or password goes. CVE-2026-40977 needs ApplicationPidFileWriter, which Spring Boot does not register for you, plus a local user who can write where the PID file goes. Check your properties for ${random.value} and your code and spring.factories for ApplicationPidFileWriter.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.fix_expected: Nothing on a line these series can take. Spring fixed both in 2.7.33, which is behind commercial support; Maven Central's last free 2.7 release is 2.7.18.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.impact: None unless the application uses ${random.value} as a secret, which is then guessable, or registers ApplicationPidFileWriter on a host where another local user can write to the PID file location, who can then corrupt one file per start.
maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.workaround: Replace any ${random.value} used as a secret with a value you generate with a secure generator and store yourself. Do not register ApplicationPidFileWriter, or point its file at a directory only the application's user can write.

maven-org-springframework-boot-spring-bo.commentary: Four Spring Boot advisories landed on this jar because the scanner matched the product name vmware:spring_boot, which every Spring Boot artifact carries. None of the four is about code in spring-boot: CVE-2026-22733 is about the Actuator CloudFoundry path, CVE-2026-40972 about DevTools, and CVE-2026-40974 and CVE-2026-41001 about the Cassandra and Artemis auto-configuration in spring-boot-autoconfigure. CVE-2026-40972 and CVE-2026-41001 are answered on those coordinates. CVE-2026-40975 and CVE-2026-40977, which are about this jar, have their own verdict.

maven-org-springframework-cloud-spring-c.commentary: This needs the writable /actuator/env endpoint, which is off unless you switch it on. Spring Cloud lets a POST to /actuator/env set any property, with no allow list of keys. spring-cloud-commons and spring-cloud-context arrive only with Control Center, and Control Center also brings Spring Boot Actuator, so the endpoint code is on your classpath. It is registered only when you set management.endpoint.env.post.enabled and expose the env endpoint over HTTP; Spring Boot exposes only health by default, and Control Center sets neither property.
maven-org-springframework-cloud-spring-c.fix_expected: The advisory fixes the 4.3 line in 4.3.4, which is published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support and not on Maven Central, whose 4.3 metadata ended at 4.3.3 when read on 2026-10-24.
maven-org-springframework-cloud-spring-c.impact: None unless the application sets management.endpoint.env.post.enabled=true and exposes the env endpoint over HTTP. Where both are true, whoever reaches the endpoint sets any property they like.
maven-org-springframework-cloud-spring-c.workaround: Leave management.endpoint.env.post.enabled unset and keep env out of management.endpoints.web.exposure.include. The 4.3 release carrying the fix, 4.3.4, is commercial from Broadcom and not on Maven Central.

maven-org-springframework-cloud-spring-c.commentary: This needs the writable /actuator/env endpoint, which is off unless you switch it on. Spring Cloud lets a POST to /actuator/env set any property, with no allow list of keys. spring-cloud-commons and spring-cloud-context arrive only with Control Center, and Control Center also brings Spring Boot Actuator, so the endpoint code is on your classpath. It is registered only when you set management.endpoint.env.post.enabled and expose the env endpoint over HTTP; Spring Boot exposes only health by default, and Control Center sets neither property.
maven-org-springframework-cloud-spring-c.fix_expected: The advisory fixes the 4.3 line in 4.3.4, which is published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support and not on Maven Central, whose 4.3 metadata ended at 4.3.3 when read on 2026-10-24.
maven-org-springframework-cloud-spring-c.impact: None unless the application sets management.endpoint.env.post.enabled=true and exposes the env endpoint over HTTP. Where both are true, whoever reaches the endpoint sets any property they like.
maven-org-springframework-cloud-spring-c.workaround: Leave management.endpoint.env.post.enabled unset and keep env out of management.endpoints.web.exposure.include. The 4.3 release carrying the fix, 4.3.4, is commercial from Broadcom and not on Maven Central.

maven-org-springframework-data-spring-da.commentary: Spring Data Commons is in your deployed application on 24.4 and 24.7, and all four need your application to accept sort, paging, property path or projection input over HTTP. vaadin-spring-boot-starter brings it through Hilla at compile scope: 3.2.12 on 24.4, 3.4.13 on 24.7, both in range. What hands request input to Spring Data is a Spring MVC controller of yours taking Pageable, Sort or a @ProjectedPayload type, or a Hilla endpoint taking Pageable. A Flow application with neither does not reach this code.
maven-org-springframework-data-spring-da.fix_expected: The releases the advisories name as fixed, 3.4.15 and later than 3.2.15, are published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support; Maven Central ends those lines at 3.4.13 and 3.2.14, read on 2026-10-24. Vaadin 24.9 and later resolve 3.5.13, which is clean.
maven-org-springframework-data-spring-da.impact: None unless the application has its own MVC controllers or Hilla endpoints that accept Pageable, Sort or projections. There an attacker exhausts the heap or the stack with crafted property paths.
maven-org-springframework-data-spring-da.workaround: The 3.2 and 3.4 releases carrying the fix are commercial from Broadcom, not on Maven Central. Setting <spring-data-bom.version>2025.0.13</spring-data-bom.version> moves it to 3.5.13, which osv.dev reports clean; that is the Spring Data generation of Spring Boot 3.5, so test your own repositories on it before shipping.

maven-org-springframework-retry-spring-r.commentary: Real where spring-retry is on the classpath, and one property clears it. A plain Vaadin 24.7 application does not resolve spring-retry; it arrives with Control Center. Where it is there, stateful retries grow a cache without bound and the advisory database puts the fix in 2.0.13, which is published on Maven Central and which it reports clean.
maven-org-springframework-retry-spring-r.fix_expected: Spring Retry 2.0.13 is already published, so nothing has to be waited for. Vaadin releases do not pin this version, Spring Boot does, and its 3.4 line ends at 3.4.13 on Maven Central, with later releases published by Broadcom under commercial Spring support.
maven-org-springframework-retry-spring-r.impact: None unless the application uses stateful retries through spring-retry, which in a Vaadin application means Control Center or a retry setup of your own. There the cache grows until the application runs out of memory.
maven-org-springframework-retry-spring-r.workaround: Set the spring-retry.version property in your own pom to 2.0.13, which the advisory database reports clean.

maven-org-springframework-security-oauth.commentary: In range on 24.4 after all, and it needs a JWT decoder your own code builds. Spring lists Spring Security 6.1.0 to 6.3.14 as affected, and 24.4.26 resolves 6.2.8. The flaw is that NimbusJwtDecoder.withIssuerLocation adds no issuer validation unless you call setJwtValidator. Spring Boot's resource server auto-configuration does call it, with an issuer validator, and nothing else on a Vaadin 24.4 classpath builds such a decoder. Search your code for withIssuerLocation; if it is there without setJwtValidator, read the workaround.

In its own words you are not affected if you do not use Spring Security's @EnableMethodSecurity, or if you do not put security annotations on methods in generic superclasses or generic interfaces. Vaadin does neither. If your own services are annotated that way, and they are reached through a generic interface, read it on your code, because there it is an authorization bypass.
maven-org-springframework-spring-core-me.impact: None from anything Vaadin registers, which is not in that shape. It needs the application to enable method security and annotate methods declared in generic superclasses or interfaces, where a call that should have been refused is allowed.
maven-org-springframework-spring-core-me.workaround: If you use @EnableMethodSecurity, put the security annotation on the concrete method rather than on the generic declaration, which is what makes the lookup unambiguous.

maven-org-springframework-spring-webmvc-.commentary: Two critical Spring MVC advisories about features a Vaadin application does not use. CVE-2026-47890 needs Server Sent Events returning view fragments, and starts at 6.2.0. Nothing on a Vaadin classpath refers to XsltView, SseEmitter or FragmentsRendering except spring-webmvc itself, and Vaadin pushes through Atmosphere. If you have MVC controllers of either shape, read these on your own code, where they are critical.
maven-org-springframework-spring-webmvc-.fix_expected: Fixed publicly only in Spring Framework 7.0.9, which needs Spring Boot 4 and so Vaadin 25. spring.io marks 6.2.20 and 6.1.29 Enterprise Support Only.
maven-org-springframework-spring-webmvc-.impact: None from Vaadin. For an application that renders XsltView under a /** mapping, CVE-2026-47884 is remote code execution: the verdict is that Vaadin does not create the condition, not that the condition is harmless.
maven-org-springframework-spring-webmvc-.workaround: If you render XSLT views, name the view explicitly rather than letting the mapping derive it from the request path. Raising the Spring Framework version from your pom does not help: the 6.1 and 6.2 releases that carry the fix exist only under Broadcom's commercial Spring support.

Six are fixed inside the 1.x line by 1.33 and the seventh, CVE-2022-1471, is the deserialisation one that is only fixed in 2.0, where SafeConstructor became the default. maven-org-yaml-snakeyaml-1-30.impact: Every Vaadin 14 and 23 application, since snakeyaml is what Spring Boot parses application.yml with. Six of the seven are denial of service through a crafted YAML document, so they matter where your application parses YAML it did not write. CVE-2022-1471 is the serious one: constructing arbitrary types from YAML, which is remote code execution wherever untrusted YAML reaches the parser.
maven-org-yaml-snakeyaml-1-30.workaround: Set the snakeyaml.version property in your own pom to 2.5. Measured on 2026-10-18 on 23.6.16: the override resolves, and by the advisory database 2.5 carries none of the seven while 1.33 still carries CVE-2022-1471. It is a major version and it changes a default rather than an API: from 2.0 the parser refuses to construct arbitrary types unless you ask it to, so an application that only lets Spring read its own application.yml is unaffected by the change, and one that deserialises its own classes from YAML has to opt back in. That is the thing to check in your application before shipping it, and it was not checked here.

maven-xerces-xercesimpl-7-8-build.commentary: The Xerces your scanner found is on your build machine and the application you deploy carries no XML parser from it at all. vaadin-maven-plugin, the plugin that compiles the widgetset on Vaadin 7 and 8, declares xercesImpl 2.10.0 directly, and all four advisories are about parsing a crafted XML document: two denials of service from 2012 and 2013, a validation flaw from the WildFly fork of the parser, and an infinite loop on a malformed payload. The XML a widgetset build reads is written by the project itself, module descriptors and plugin configuration in your own source tree, not anything an outside party sends. The war you deploy resolves no Xerces on any path.
maven-xerces-xercesimpl-7-8-build.impact: None in a deployed application: it carries no Xerces. On the build machine the four need the build to parse an XML document somebody hostile wrote, and what the widgetset compilation parses is your own project files.

Charts calls sanitize with no options, so advisories that need SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES, IN_PLACE, PARSER_MEDIA_TYPE or a hook are never met by Vaadin's call. npm-esbuild-dev-server.commentary: esbuild is part of what builds your frontend and of nothing you deploy, and this advisory is about its development server. npm-glob-abort-signal-24.commentary: The defect is that a glob walk keeps reading directories after its AbortSignal has fired, which only matters to a caller that relies on a signal to bound how much work a walk does. Nothing in a Vaadin build passes one. glob runs on the build machine, called by the theme plugins of flow and by workbox-build on the output directory, always through globSync and never with a signal, and it is not in the bundle the browser loads.
npm-glob-abort-signal-24.impact: None unless your own build code passes an AbortSignal to glob to limit a walk. There, the walk keeps reading the file system after it was cancelled.

npm-highcharts-14-options-xss-2026-10-30.commentary: Highcharts is what Vaadin Charts draws with, so this reaches the browser, and every advisory here needs chart options carrying text from an untrusted source. Vaadin Charts 6.3.8 already applies the mitigation the first advisory recommends: it wraps Highcharts.chart, stockChart and the chart, axis, series and legend update methods and runs DOMPurify over every string in the options. Markup in a title or label is therefore stripped unless it bypasses DOMPurify 2.5.7. A link is not markup, so a javascript: URL placed in a link option is not removed by that: the second advisory, and CVE-2026-118251 for credits.href. Credits.setHref in the Java API checks the scheme against the safeUrlSchemes property, which allows every scheme unless you set it. CVE-2026-118250 writes to Object.prototype through a dotted path in series.keys, which only your code sets, through setKeys on the plot options, and Vaadin Charts never sets it. The Vaadin fix for the 2026 advisories, CVE-2026-107588, starts at Vaadin 23 and does not cover this line.
npm-highcharts-14-options-xss-2026-10-30.fix_expected: Nothing on this line: the 14 line resolves highcharts 6.1.4 through @vaadin/vaadin-charts 6.3.8, which pins it exactly, and the fixes are 7.2.2 and 9.0.0, and 11.4.9 for CVE-2026-118250 and CVE-2026-118251.
npm-highcharts-14-options-xss-2026-10-30.impact: None unless the application builds chart link options or series keys from user input. There a viewer who clicks the link runs script, a crafted keys path writes to Object.prototype in the viewer's page, and text options are exposed only through a DOMPurify 2.5.7 bypass.
npm-highcharts-14-options-xss-2026-10-30.workaround: Build link targets and series keys in chart options only from values you control. For links set through the Java API, set the safeUrlSchemes property to http,https so setHref refuses any other scheme.

npm-minimatch-globparts-24.commentary: The code is there: minimatch 9.0.9 and 10.2.6 carry the pattern optimiser the advisory describes, and glob calls it with optimizationLevel 2. What it needs is an attacker who chooses the glob pattern, and in a Vaadin build nobody outside the project does. minimatch runs only on the build machine, under glob and workbox-build, and is not in the bundle the browser loads. The patterns it is handed are fixed by Vaadin, **/* for the service worker and *.css for the theme, or written by the developer in the assets section of their own theme.json. 5.1.9, the other copy on these lines, predates the optimiser.
npm-minimatch-globparts-24.impact: None unless your own build code passes a glob pattern that someone outside your team can choose to glob or minimatch. There, a crafted pattern makes the build spend excessive CPU and memory.

npm-node-forge-14-dev-server.commentary: node-forge is here only so the development server can make itself a self signed certificate. It arrives under selfsigned, which arrives under webpack-dev-server, which Vaadin writes into devDependencies, and it is not in the bundle the browser loads. The development server Vaadin configures speaks plain http and never loads selfsigned at all. Even where an application switches it to https, selfsigned only generates a fresh key pair and a certificate for localhost and checks that certificate against itself: nothing it does verifies an RSA signature from elsewhere, decodes a PEM it was given, opens a TLS connection, reads PKCS#12, handles cookies, decrypts anything or verifies an Ed25519 signature, which is where these advisories live. node-forge 1.4.1 fixes the eleven published in October 2026 and five of the nine published in November, and 1.4.3 fixes the other four; selfsigned accepts any 1.x, so a build that installs its npm packages again picks up the fixed version.
npm-node-forge-14-dev-server.impact: None unless your own build code calls node-forge directly; the library only runs on the build machine, and in the development server Vaadin configures it does not run at all.

npm-opentelemetry-core.commentary: The package is there and the vulnerable code is not reached. The advisory is about W3CBaggagePropagator.extract, which parses baggage headers arriving from somewhere else. A Vaadin application uses the browser SDK to start its own spans and never extracts inbound baggage, so that function is not on any execution path.
npm-opentelemetry-core.impact: None without an application that extracts baggage headers from incoming requests.

npm-path-to-regexp-router-pattern.commentary: This needs a route of a particular shape, and it hangs the visitor's own browser rather than your server. path-to-regexp turns a route pattern into a regular expression, and it produces a backtracking one whenever a single segment holds two parameters separated by anything other than a dot, as in /:a-:b. A path crafted against such a pattern then takes a very long time to match. It reaches a Vaadin application through @vaadin/router, the client side router, so the matching happens in the browser: what stops is the tab of whoever followed the link. Look at your own route patterns for two parameters in one segment. If there are none, there is no regular expression of that kind to attack.
npm-path-to-regexp-router-pattern.fix_expected: Upstream fixes it in 3.3.0 and the lockfile of 24.4.25 resolves 2.4.0, pinned by @vaadin/router at exactly that version, so no rebuilt bundle takes it: somebody has to move the number in @vaadin/router.
npm-path-to-regexp-router-pattern.impact: None on the server, because the matching runs in the browser, and none at all unless the application declares a route with two parameters in one segment. There a visitor who opens a crafted link sees their own tab stop responding.
npm-path-to-regexp-router-pattern.workaround: Separate two parameters in one segment with a dot, or put them in segments of their own, which is what the upstream fix advises for patterns that cannot be changed.

npm-quill-2021-3163.commentary: The flaw is real in the Quill that Rich Text Editor bundles, and Vaadin keeps the payload away from it. Every 24 release carries Quill 1.3.6, inside the advisory, and that Quill runs an IMG event handler when it is handed raw HTML. RichTextEditor cleans every value with jsoup in both directions, on what a browser sends and on what setValue shows, and no on* attribute survives. You are exposed only if your code puts HTML into the editor another way: callJsFunction or executeJs with dangerouslySetHtmlValue, or the vaadin-rich-text-editor element used from client code with HTML someone else wrote.
npm-quill-2021-3163.fix_expected: None upstream: GHSA-4943-9vgg-gr5r says no patch exists and no further Quill 1 releases are planned.
npm-quill-2021-3163.impact: None through RichTextEditor.setValue or the editor itself, which clean the HTML. HTML that reaches the editor in the browser without that cleaning can run script in the browser of whoever views it.
npm-quill-2021-3163.workaround: Nothing, if HTML reaches the editor only through RichTextEditor.setValue or what users type. If your code calls dangerouslySetHtmlValue or feeds the element from client code, pass the HTML through RichTextEditor.setValue instead, or clean it with jsoup first.

npm-quill-2025-15056-from-25-3-5.commentary: Fixed on this line. Platform 25.3.5 pins @vaadin/rich-text-editor 25.3.5, whose vendored Quill escapes the video and formula values before building the semantic HTML, and the reproduction that fires on 25.3.4 does not fire here. The patched copy keeps Quill's own version string 2.0.3, because the fix is ours and there is no Quill release to move to, so a scanner reading the bundled file reports the advisory on this version anyway. That report is stale, not a second finding. CVE-2026-120350 names this same flaw: it is the advisory Vaadin itself published for it, and CVE-2025-15056 is the id under which it was first reported, so a scanner may lead with either. One record, one fix, and this verdict answers both ids.
npm-quill-2025-15056-from-25-3-5.fix_expected: Already in. Released in @vaadin/rich-text-editor 25.3.5 on 2026-10-29 and pinned by platform 25.3.5.
npm-quill-2025-15056-from-25-3-5.impact: None on 25.3.5 and later: the version you are running carries the corrected copy. Below 25.3.5 the editor is affected through RichTextEditor.asDelta(), which has its own verdict.
npm-quill-2025-15056-from-25-3-5.workaround: None needed. A scanner that still reports it is reading Quill's version string rather than the code.
