npm-react-router-open-redirect.commentary: A path beginning with a backslash can be read by the browser as an address on another site, and React Router 6 passes it through. Every way Vaadin itself hands a path to the router is guarded before the router sees it: a click on a link is dropped unless the anchor's origin equals the window's, and then again unless its href starts with the document's base URI, and both checks are done by the browser's own URL parser, which resolves a backslash the same way the address bar would. The one path that is not guarded is the one your server chooses, because there Vaadin navigates where the application told it to. So the question is your own code: if you call UI.navigate, or set a location, with a value that came from a query parameter, a form field or a database row an attacker can write, then that value can take the browser off your site. Validate it before you navigate, the way you would validate any redirect target.
npm-react-router-open-redirect.fix_expected: None on this line, and the line above has already made the move. osv.dev puts the fix at 7.18.0 for both, a major version, and measured on 2026-10-19 the dev bundle of 24.7.16 resolves react-router 7.18.3 and those of 24.9.23 and 24.10.11 resolve 7.18.4, with react-router-dom gone from the root dependencies entirely. 24.4 stays on 6.30.6 because taking React Router 7 into a maintained line would change the API Flow's own router code is written against.
npm-react-router-open-redirect.impact: None for an application that only navigates to its own routes, which is every application that has not written that code. One that navigates to a location built from user input is exposed to the ordinary open redirect: a visitor who follows a crafted link ends up on somebody else's site with your application's name in the referrer, which is a phishing step rather than a way into your data.
npm-react-router-open-redirect.workaround: Check any navigation target that came from outside before passing it on: reject a value that starts with a slash or a backslash followed by another slash or backslash, and prefer naming the route class or a fixed path over passing a string through. There is nothing to configure in Vaadin for this.

npm-react-router-ssr-hydration.commentary: This one is about server side rendering, which a Vaadin application does not do. The advisory says so in its own words: it does not affect Declarative Mode and only impacts Framework Mode and Data Mode applications doing manual SSR and hydration. Flow's React integration renders in the browser and nothing else: its frontend sources contain no hydrateRoot, no StaticRouter, no createStaticHandler and no reference to deserializeErrors, which is the function the advisory is about. You would have to write your own server rendering around React Router, outside anything Vaadin generates, and then let attacker input shape the errors it serialises.
npm-react-router-ssr-hydration.fix_expected: None on this line, and the line above has already made the move. osv.dev puts the fix at 7.18.0 for both, a major version, and measured on 2026-10-19 the dev bundle of 24.7.16 resolves react-router 7.18.3 and those of 24.9.23 and 24.10.11 resolve 7.18.4, with react-router-dom gone from the root dependencies entirely. 24.4 stays on 6.30.6 because taking React Router 7 into a maintained line would change the API Flow's own router code is written against.
npm-react-router-ssr-hydration.impact: None as Vaadin renders. The advisory itself calls the application code that would be needed very specific and unlikely, and it is code nobody writes inside a Flow application.

npm-serialize-javascript-14-23-build-plu.commentary: serialize-javascript runs while your frontend is built and is in nothing you deploy. On 14 it arrives under compression-webpack-plugin and copy-webpack-plugin, on 23 under rollup-plugin-terser inside workbox-build, the service worker builder, and Vaadin declares those as development dependencies. CVE-2026-34043 is CPU exhaustion on a crafted array like object and needs an attacker to shape what the build serialises, which is the build's own data. CVE-2020-7660 does not apply: it is fixed in 3.1.0, and 14 resolves 6.0.2 and 23 resolves 4.0.0.

npm-serialize-javascript-build-tool-14-2.commentary: serialize-javascript turns build time data into JavaScript source while your frontend is built, and it is in nothing you deploy. Both advisories are cross site scripting through a closing script tag left unescaped, which matters when the serialised value comes from somebody else and lands in a page. On 14 it arrives under compression-webpack-plugin and copy-webpack-plugin, on 23 under rollup-plugin-terser inside workbox-build; Vaadin declares those as development dependencies, so what it serialises is build output.

npm-uuid-14-dev-server.commentary: A missing bounds check when a caller passes its own buffer to the v3, v5 or v6 generators. It reaches a Vaadin 14 build under sockjs, the WebSocket fallback of the development server, and not through anything the browser loads. Nothing in a Vaadin application calls those generators at all, let alone with a buffer of its own.
npm-uuid-14-dev-server.impact: None. The package is on the build machine, under the development server.

npm-vite-build-tool.commentary: Vite builds your frontend and is not part of it: Vaadin names it as a development dependency, and the archive you deploy carries the bundle it produced, not vite. All thirteen are about its development server: ten let it serve files outside its server.fs rules, two are in the editor launcher it offers, a command injection and an NTLMv2 hash leak, both on Windows, and one lets any website the developer visits send it requests and read the answers. They matter on a developer machine while that server runs.
npm-vite-build-tool.fix_expected: None on 23.6 and 24.4: Vaadin names vite 3.2.11 and 5.4.21 exactly there, and the three left on 24.4 are fixed only from vite 6.4.2 and 6.4.3.
npm-vite-build-tool.impact: None in a deployed application. On a developer machine running the development server, another site or request can read project files or, on Windows, run a command or leak a hash.
npm-vite-build-tool.workaround: Nothing for what you deploy. On the developer machine, 24.7.16, 24.9.19 and 24.10.7 or later resolve versions outside all thirteen; 24.4.26 still matches three and 23.6.17 all thirteen.

npm-vite-dev-server-2026-10-22.commentary: Nothing you deploy runs vite: Vaadin names it as a development dependency, a production build runs it once to make the bundle, and the archive carries the bundle. All five are about the development server. Three are in launch-editor, which that server uses to open a file in your editor from the error overlay; one is script execution through custom middleware, and one serves files outside server.fs.allow on a server exposed to the network. Each needs that server running plus the condition its advisory states.
npm-vite-dev-server-2026-10-22.fix_expected: Not on 23.6, 24.4, 24.7 or 24.9 yet. Vaadin names vite exactly, so a rebuilt lockfile never takes a fix on its own: 24.9.24 still pins 7.3.6 and 24.7.17 pins 6.4.3, one patch below 7.3.7 and 6.4.4, published 2026-10-06, and the 3.2 and 5.4 lines that 23.6 and 24.4 pin have no fixed release.
npm-vite-dev-server-2026-10-22.impact: None in a deployed application. On a developer machine, two of the launch-editor advisories need Windows and the third needs an editor such as Vim or Emacs and a file named with a leading plus or minus sign.
npm-vite-dev-server-2026-10-22.workaround: Upgrade within your line where a release carries the fix: 24.10.12 resolves vite 7.3.7, 25.2.12 and 25.3.3 resolve 8.3.4. An overrides entry for launch-editor changes nothing, because vite compiles it into its own files.

npm-webpack-14-buildhttp.commentary: webpack is what bundles your frontend and is in nothing you deploy, and both advisories are about a webpack feature that a Vaadin build does not use. They are ways around the allowedUris list of buildHttp, the option that lets a build fetch modules over HTTP, one through a redirect and one through userinfo in the URL. A Vaadin build resolves its modules from the npm registry and the project, not over buildHttp, and the result either way is a request made by the build machine.
npm-webpack-14-buildhttp.impact: None in a deployed application. On a build machine, only for a build that turns buildHttp on and relies on allowedUris to bound it, which a Vaadin build does not.

npm-webpack-dev-server-14.commentary: This is the development server, and all four advisories are about it serving a developer. One lets another website in the developer's browser forge requests to its internal endpoints, one lets any origin read source over a non HTTPS connection, one intercepts the hot reload WebSocket through a permissive proxy, and one kills it with a malformed Host header. None of that exists in a deployed application: the server is started by the development build and the thing a production build produces is the bundle. Vaadin writes webpack-dev-server into the devDependencies of the generated package.json itself.
npm-webpack-dev-server-14.impact: None in a deployed application. On a developer's machine, a website open in another tab can read the source being worked on or drive the reload channel.
